books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — The Progressive Movement, Race, and Segregation
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20.
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20: Most white Progressives accepted the segregation of the Jim Crow South and did little for Black Americans. President Woodrow Wilson allowed his cabinet to resegregate federal offices, and he praised the film Birth of a Nation (1915). Black reformers organized for themselves: W. E. B. Du Bois helped found the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in 1909 to demand full equality. Black women pursued the same reforms as white women, temperance, education, and uplift, but their work left few written records and stayed nearly invisible in histories of the movement. Women's suffrage, organized since the National American Woman Suffrage Association formed in 1890, finally won the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.

source: original; stimulus paraphrased from 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9
stem: According to the passage, Black women's progressivism stayed 'nearly invisible' in histories mainly because

options.text: their activism began only after the 1920s had ended
options.misconception: Their work ran through the Progressive Era itself, from the 1890s to 1920, not after it.

options.text: Black women generally opposed the Progressive movement and all of its goals
options.misconception: They pursued the same goals as white women: temperance, education, and uplift.

options.text: their work left few written records
white Progressives carefully documented Black women's contributions in writing
options.misconception: White reformers largely ignored Black women's parallel work; that silence is the point.

rationales.A: Black women's reform work ran through the Progressive Era, not after it. The passage places it beside white women's reform work of the same years.
rationales.B: Black women took up the same reforms white women pursued: temperance, education, and uplift. They did not oppose the movement's goals.
rationales.C: The passage says their work left few written records and stayed nearly invisible in histories. Historians working from the paper trail wrote them out: an absence of sources, not an absence of activism.
rationales.D: White reformers did not document Black women's work. The passage says it stayed nearly invisible, which is the opposite of careful documentation.
rationales.general:
1. Read the passage's explanation. Black women pursued the same reforms as white women, but their work left few written records.
2. Follow the consequence. Histories follow the records, so work that left few records stayed nearly invisible.
3. Name the cause. Invisibility came from missing archives, not from missing activism.
Remember: history is written from what survives, so ask whose papers were kept before deciding who was absent.
